author: reek
body: A `when` keeps every `is` arm written on a line, however the arms are packed across lines.

author: reek
body: The parser accepts an arm that starts on the same line as the arm before it, or at the column the arms are aligned on. `ln` used to be pinned to the line the match STARTED on and never advanced, so `tok.line == ln` could not hold again once the arms reached a second line -- and the arm that matched neither test ended the match in silence.

author: reek
body: The measured shape was not the "one arm per line" the entry described. Every arm on the FIRST line parsed, the FIRST arm of the second line parsed, and the second arm of the second line ended the `when` -- taking every later line with it. `many-per-line` below is that exact case: it kept `is 1`, `is 2`, `is 3` and silently dropped `is 4`, `is 5`, `is 6` AND the `is otherwise`, with no diagnostic of any kind.

author: reek
body: Both directions are pinned here because the two lines fail differently. `one-line` always worked (its arms share the match's own line) and must keep working. `many-per-line` is the regression, and its `is otherwise` matters most: a dropped catch-all leaves a `when` with no arm for its own default, and on an open type like Integer nothing is checking.

author: reek
body: Exhaustiveness was the only thing that ever caught this, and only on a closed variant -- which is why the one site anybody found (`Dev`'s GamepadManager, CL 8333) was a closed variant and everything else went unnoticed. This test uses Integer on purpose: no exhaustiveness check can stand in for the parser here.
